title: Typhoons
standard_code: Grade 8, Quarter 3: Earth and Space Science
standard_text: Tropical cyclones form over warm oceans from low pressure areas; their structure (eye, eyewall, rain bands); categories and PAGASA Tropical Cyclone Wind Signals; hazards (strong winds, flooding, storm surge, landslides); preparedness. (summary of the MATATAG Science curriculum, Grade 8, Quarter 3: Earth and Space Science)
meta_desc: Free Grade 8 Science worksheets (MATATAG, Quarter 3: Earth and Space Science): how typhoons form, the parts of a typhoon, categories and wind signals, storm surge and preparedness. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Typhoons get their energy from warm ocean water.
key_sub: Higher wind signals mean stronger winds coming sooner.
body_html:
How to think about it

A typhoon begins as a low pressure area over warm ocean water. Warm, moist air rises, cools and forms clouds; air rushes in to replace it and the Earth's rotation makes the storm spin counterclockwise. The calm eye is surrounded by the eyewall, where winds are strongest.

PAGASA classifies tropical cyclones from tropical depression to super typhoon and raises Tropical Cyclone Wind Signals No. 1 to No. 5. Typhoons bring strong winds, heavy rain, floods, landslides and storm surges. Families prepare with go bags, evacuation plans and by following official warnings.

Example

Where is the calmest part of a typhoon?

The center

Answer: the eye

Example

Why does a typhoon weaken over land?

Energy source

Answer: it loses warm, moist ocean air

Common mistakes

  • Thinking the danger is over when the eye passes.
  • Thinking the wind signal tells the amount of rain.
  • Ignoring storm surge warnings on the coast.

faq.q: What made Typhoon Yolanda (Haiyan) so destructive?
faq.a: Extremely strong winds and a storm surge several meters high flooded coastal towns in 2013.

faq.q: Why do typhoons spin counterclockwise in the Philippines?
faq.a: The Earth's rotation deflects winds in the Northern Hemisphere.

items.q: What is an aquifer?
c: a layer of porous, permeable rock that holds and transmits groundwater
items.e: Sandstone is often a good aquifer.

items.q: What happens to the surplus of energy at the tropics?
c: it is lost into space at once
winds and ocean currents carry it towards the poles
it is stored in the core
items.e: This drives global circulation.

items.q: What is the calm center of a typhoon called?
items.e: The eye has light winds and few clouds; the strongest winds are in the eyewall around it.

items.q: What is infiltration?
items.e: It is greater in sandy soil than clay.

items.q: Why does a forest have a lower albedo than a desert?
c: dark leaves absorb more sunlight than pale sand
items.e: Clearing forests can change local climate.

items.q: What drives thermohaline circulation in the oceans?
c: differences in water density caused by temperature and salinity
items.e: Cold, salty water sinks near Antarctica.

items.q: Which agency gives typhoon warnings in the Philippines?
items.e: PAGASA is the weather bureau of the Philippines.

items.q: Where are the strongest winds of a typhoon?
c: in the eyewall, around the eye
items.e: The eyewall has the strongest winds and heaviest rain.

items.q: What is upwelling?
c: cold, nutrient-rich deep water rising to the surface
items.e: Upwelling areas are very productive fisheries.

items.q: What is the enhanced greenhouse effect?
c: extra warming caused by greenhouse gases added by human activity
the warming caused by the Sun getting hotter
the natural warming that keeps Earth habitable
items.e: CO₂ from fossil fuels is the main cause.

items.q: Why does a typhoon weaken when it moves over land?
c: it loses its supply of warm, moist air from the ocean
items.e: Typhoons get their energy from warm ocean water.

items.q: Where do typhoons form?
items.e: Warm, moist air over the ocean gives the storm its energy.

items.q: How does the greenhouse effect work?
c: greenhouse gases absorb infrared radiation from Earth's surface and re-emit some back down
items.e: Without it Earth would average about −18 °C.

items.q: What are the two main sources of energy for Earth processes?
c: solar radiation and Earth's internal heat
items.e: Internal heat drives plate tectonics; solar energy drives weather.

items.q: How does heat move through the mantle?
c: mostly by convection: hot rock slowly rises and cooler rock sinks
items.e: Convection takes millions of years.

items.q: Which energy source drives the water cycle?
items.e: Evaporation needs energy.

items.q: What is a Hadley cell?
c: a circulation in which warm air rises near the Equator and sinks near 30° latitude
an ocean current along the Equator
items.e: There are Hadley, Ferrel and polar cells.

items.q: What is a typhoon?
c: a cold wind from the north
a strong earthquake under the sea
a strong tropical cyclone with very strong winds and heavy rain
items.e: Typhoons form over warm ocean water.

items.q: Which part of the water cycle returns most water from land to the atmosphere in a forest?
items.e: Trees release water vapor through their leaves.

items.q: Why is the stratosphere warmer at the top than at the bottom?
c: it is closer to Earth's core
ozone absorbs ultraviolet radiation from the Sun
the air is denser at the top
items.e: In the troposphere temperature falls with height.

items.q: Emmanuel learns that an air mass formed over the North Pacific. What will it most likely be like?
items.e: Air masses take on the temperature and humidity of where they form: over cold ocean water.

items.q: What is a low pressure area (LPA)?
c: a region where air pressure is lower than around it, which may develop into a tropical cyclone
a place with very cold air
items.e: Air rises in an LPA and clouds form.

items.q: Rafael learns that an air mass formed over the Gulf of Mexico. What will it most likely be like?
items.e: Air masses take on the temperature and humidity of where they form: over warm ocean water near the equator.

items.q: Vincent learns that an air mass formed over the cold North Atlantic. What will it most likely be like?
items.e: Air masses take on the temperature and humidity of where they form: over cold ocean water.

items.q: Angel's forecast says a warm front is coming. What weather should Angel expect?
c: Light, steady rain or drizzle, then warmer and more humid weather.
Many days of cloudy, wet weather.
Thunderstorms or heavy rain, then cooler and drier weather.
items.e: A warm air mass slides up over a cold air mass.

items.q: Rodel reads about a hot and dry air mass. Where did it most likely form?
items.e: A continental tropical air mass forms over hot, dry land.

items.q: Isabel sees a big L (low pressure) over the town on the weather map. What weather is likely?
c: dry, calm weather for a week
items.e: Rising air in a low-pressure area cools and forms clouds.

items.q: Rose reads: “A warm air mass slides up over a cold air mass.” What kind of front is this?
items.e: That describes a warm front.

items.q: About how many tropical cyclones enter the Philippine Area of Responsibility each year?
items.e: The Philippines is one of the most typhoon-prone countries.

items.q: Rafael's barometer reading has been rising after a storm. What does this suggest?
items.e: Rising pressure often means a high-pressure system is arriving.

items.q: Trisha sees a big H (high pressure) over the town on the weather map. What weather is likely?
items.e: Sinking air in a high-pressure area keeps clouds from forming.

items.q: Why do typhoons in the Philippines spin counterclockwise?
c: because of the Earth's rotation in the Northern Hemisphere
because the wind comes from mountains
items.e: The Coriolis effect makes storms spin counterclockwise north of the equator.

items.q: Miguel learns that an air mass formed over the Pacific near Hawaii. What will it most likely be like?
items.e: Air masses take on the temperature and humidity of where they form: over warm ocean water near the equator.

items.q: Christian reads: “A cold front catches up to a warm front and lifts the warm air off the ground.” What kind of front is this?
items.e: That describes an occluded front.

items.q: Dennis reads about a warm and humid air mass. Where did it most likely form?
items.e: A maritime tropical air mass forms over warm ocean water near the equator.

items.q: Jasmine's forecast says a cold front is coming. What weather should Jasmine expect?
c: Light, steady rain or drizzle, then warmer and more humid weather.
Many days of cloudy, wet weather.
Thunderstorms or heavy rain, then cooler and drier weather.
items.e: A cold air mass pushes under a warm air mass and forces it up quickly.

items.q: Nico's forecast says an occluded front is coming. What weather should Nico expect?
c: Thunderstorms or heavy rain, then cooler and drier weather.
Light, steady rain or drizzle, then warmer and more humid weather.
Many days of cloudy, wet weather.
items.e: A cold front catches up to a warm front and lifts the warm air off the ground.

items.q: Kenneth reads: “A cold air mass pushes under a warm air mass and forces it up quickly.” What kind of front is this?
items.e: That describes a cold front.

items.q: Which is the correct order as a storm grows stronger?
c: tropical depression → tropical storm → severe tropical storm → typhoon → super typhoon
items.e: PAGASA classifies tropical cyclones by wind speed.

items.q: Kenneth learns that an air mass formed over the deserts of the Southwest. What will it most likely be like?
items.e: Air masses take on the temperature and humidity of where they form: over hot, dry land.

items.q: What is a climate model?
c: a physical model of a volcano
a computer model that uses physics to simulate the climate and project future changes
a list of past temperatures only
items.e: Models are tested against past climate.

items.q: What is adaptation to climate change?
c: changing how we live to cope with its effects, such as building sea walls or planting heat-tolerant crops
items.e: Both mitigation and adaptation are needed.

items.q: A community plans drainage and retaining walls on steep slopes. Which hazard is this mainly meant to reduce?
items.e: Match the plan to the hazard.

items.q: Which observation is evidence of warmer, earlier springs?
c: Shells of sea snails grow thinner in more acidic water.
Corals turn white and die in hot summers.
Spring flowers bloom and birds migrate earlier than 50 years ago.
items.e: Match the evidence to the change.

items.q: Which action best reduces the risk to people from volcanic eruptions?
c: building codes that make structures flexible and strong
drainage and retaining walls on steep slopes
monitoring gas and ground swelling to warn people
ocean sensors linked to warning sirens
items.e: Hazards cannot be stopped, but their harm can be reduced.

items.q: Which action best reduces the risk to people from wildfires?
c: drainage and retaining walls on steep slopes
zoning that keeps homes off the floodplain
monitoring gas and ground swelling to warn people
clearing brush to make defensible space around homes
items.e: Hazards cannot be stopped, but their harm can be reduced.

items.q: Which action best reduces the risk to people from landslides?
c: drainage and retaining walls on steep slopes
building codes that make structures flexible and strong
ocean sensors linked to warning sirens
monitoring gas and ground swelling to warn people
items.e: Hazards cannot be stopped, but their harm can be reduced.

items.q: Which Tropical Cyclone Wind Signal is the highest?
items.e: PAGASA uses Signals No. 1 to No. 5.

items.q: A community plans zoning that keeps homes off the floodplain. Which hazard is this mainly meant to reduce?
items.e: Match the plan to the hazard.

items.q: Which action best reduces the risk to people from river floods?
c: ocean sensors linked to warning sirens
building codes that make structures flexible and strong
monitoring gas and ground swelling to warn people
zoning that keeps homes off the floodplain
items.e: Hazards cannot be stopped, but their harm can be reduced.

items.q: What is the difference between weather and climate?
c: weather is short-term conditions; climate is the average pattern over decades
items.e: Climate is often averaged over 30 years.

items.q: Spring flowers bloom and birds migrate earlier than 50 years ago. Which climate change is this evidence of?
items.e: Many independent kinds of evidence point the same way.

items.q: Which item should be in an emergency go bag?
c: a flashlight, water, food, medicine and a radio
items.e: A go bag helps a family survive the first days after a disaster.

items.q: What is a storm surge?
c: an abnormal rise of sea water pushed onto land by a typhoon's winds
a wave made by a ship
items.e: Storm surges can flood coastal areas, as in Typhoon Yolanda (Haiyan) in 2013.

items.q: Mountain glaciers worldwide are shrinking. Which climate change is this evidence of?
items.e: Many independent kinds of evidence point the same way.

items.q: Why should families near rivers evacuate during a strong typhoon?
c: heavy rain can cause floods and flash floods
items.e: Heavy rain raises river levels quickly.

items.q: What does Tropical Cyclone Wind Signal No. 1 mean?
c: the strongest winds are expected within 12 hours
there is no danger at all
strong winds are expected within 36 hours
items.e: Higher signal numbers mean stronger winds coming sooner.

items.q: Which action best reduces the risk to people from tsunamis?
c: drainage and retaining walls on steep slopes
clearing brush to make defensible space around homes
building codes that make structures flexible and strong
ocean sensors linked to warning sirens
items.e: Hazards cannot be stopped, but their harm can be reduced.

items.q: Some plants and animals are moving uphill and toward the poles. Which climate change is this evidence of?
items.e: Many independent kinds of evidence point the same way.

items.q: Why are many typhoons given local names by PAGASA?
c: because each one has a different eye
so that people can easily identify and remember each storm
items.e: Local names help people follow warnings.

items.q: Lorna's town wants to reduce damage from earthquakes. Which technology would help most?
c: ocean buoys and warning sirens with marked evacuation routes
levees, floodplain maps and raised buildings
buildings with base isolators and flexible steel frames
gas and tilt sensors with evacuation plans
items.e: Mitigation technology matches the hazard.

items.q: Which instrument measures wind speed?
items.e: Its cups spin faster in stronger wind.

items.q: What happens to the air pressure as a typhoon comes closer?
items.e: A barometer shows falling pressure when a storm is near.

items.q: Which usually happens faster: a sand dune moving across a desert or an ocean basin opening?
c: a sand dune moving across a desert
They take exactly the same time.
items.e: Earth processes range from seconds to hundreds of millions of years.

items.q: Hazel's town tried storm drains that carry water away to protect against floods. Which claim does the data support?
c: The solution made the damage worse.
The solution stopped floods from happening.
items.e: Homes flooded went from 48 to 20. The hazard still happens, but it does less damage.

items.q: Which instrument shows the direction the wind is coming from?
items.e: The arrow points to where the wind is coming from.

items.q: Camille's town often has blizzards. Which solution would best reduce the damage from blizzards?
c: drip hoses that water roots slowly
keeping extra blankets and food at home
surge protectors for computers and TVs
items.e: Keeping extra blankets and food at home helps with blizzards.

items.q: Diane sees a town using building an underground storm shelter. Which weather hazard is this mainly for?
items.e: This solution reduces the impact of tornadoes.

items.q: Rica's town tried building a levee along the river. How many fewer homes flooded were there after the solution?
Emmanuel's town wants to reduce damage from hurricanes. Which technology would help most?
c: buildings with base isolators and flexible steel frames
storm shutters, stronger roof straps and early warnings from satellites
ocean buoys and warning sirens with marked evacuation routes
retaining walls, drainage and planting trees on slopes
items.e: Mitigation technology matches the hazard.

items.q: Rose's town tried putting storm shutters over windows to protect against hurricanes. Which claim does the data support?
c: The solution stopped hurricanes from happening.
The solution made the damage worse.
items.e: Homes damaged went from 25 to 10. The hazard still happens, but it does less damage.

items.q: Carmela sees a town using strapping roofs tightly to the walls. Which weather hazard is this mainly for?
items.e: This solution reduces the impact of hurricanes.

items.q: Which months bring the most typhoons to the Philippines?
items.e: Most typhoons come during the wet (rainy) season.

items.q: Sheila's town often has tornadoes. Which solution would best reduce the damage from tornadoes?
c: surge protectors for computers and TVs
drip hoses that water roots slowly
a safe room with strong concrete walls
planting a rain garden that soaks up water
items.e: A safe room with strong concrete walls helps with tornadoes.

items.q: Kristine sees a town using fixing leaky pipes to save water. Which weather hazard is this mainly for?
items.e: This solution reduces the impact of droughts.

items.q: Arnel's town tried strapping roofs tightly to the walls. How many fewer homes damaged were there after the solution?
Rose's town often has lightning. Which solution would best reduce the damage from lightning?
c: planting a rain garden that soaks up water
strapping roofs tightly to the walls
planting crops that need little water
items.e: Going indoors when thunder roars helps with lightning.

items.q: Vincent's town tried building a levee along the river to protect against floods. Which claim does the data support?
c: The solution stopped floods from happening.
The solution made the damage worse.
items.e: Homes flooded went from 59 to 48. The hazard still happens, but it does less damage.

items.q: Joshua sees a town using a lightning rod on the roof. Which weather hazard is this mainly for?
items.e: This solution reduces the impact of lightning.

items.q: Diane's town wants to reduce damage from volcanic eruptions. Which technology would help most?
c: gas and tilt sensors with evacuation plans
storm shutters, stronger roof straps and early warnings from satellites
cleared defensible space around homes and fire-resistant roofs
retaining walls, drainage and planting trees on slopes
items.e: Mitigation technology matches the hazard.

items.q: In Nico's model, warming is now 1 °C above the pre-industrial level and rising 0.3 °C per decade. If this rate continues, about how warm will it be in 30 years?
Lance reads that sea level is rising about 5 mm per year. At this rate, how much will it rise in 10 years?
Rafael reads that sea level is rising about 5 mm per year. At this rate, how much will it rise in 50 years?
In Gabriel's model, warming is now 1.2 °C above the pre-industrial level and rising 0.25 °C per decade. If this rate continues, about how warm will it be in 40 years?
In Joshua's model, warming is now 1 °C above the pre-industrial level and rising 0.3 °C per decade. If this rate continues, about how warm will it be in 50 years?
What is latent heat's role in weather?
c: energy taken up in evaporation is released when water vapor condenses in clouds, powering storms
items.e: Tropical cyclones are fueled by latent heat.

items.q: A tide gauge in Nicole's town shows sea level rose 8 cm in 10 years. What is the average rate?
items.e: 8 cm = 80 mm; 80 ÷ 10 = 8 mm per year.

items.q: In Mae's model, warming is now 1.3 °C above the pre-industrial level and rising 0.2 °C per decade. If this rate continues, about how warm will it be in 50 years?
A tide gauge in Rafael's town shows sea level rose 3 cm in 10 years. What is the average rate?
items.e: 3 cm = 30 mm; 30 ÷ 10 = 3 mm per year.

items.q: In Bianca's model, warming is now 1 °C above the pre-industrial level and rising 0.4 °C per decade. If this rate continues, about how warm will it be in 20 years?
A tide gauge in Lorna's town shows sea level rose 17.5 cm in 50 years. What is the average rate?
Bryan reads that sea level is rising about 5 mm per year. At this rate, how much will it rise in 20 years?
In Diane's model, warming is now 1.1 °C above the pre-industrial level and rising 0.4 °C per decade. If this rate continues, about how warm will it be in 40 years?
In Mae's model, warming is now 1.2 °C above the pre-industrial level and rising 0.25 °C per decade. If this rate continues, about how warm will it be in 30 years?
In Rodel's model, warming is now 1 °C above the pre-industrial level and rising 0.25 °C per decade. If this rate continues, about how warm will it be in 30 years?
In Maria's model, warming is now 1 °C above the pre-industrial level and rising 0.25 °C per decade. If this rate continues, about how warm will it be in 20 years?
Why is Earth's internal heat still flowing out after 4.5 billion years?
c: radioactive isotopes keep producing heat, and the deep interior holds heat from Earth's formation
items.e: Uranium-238 has a half-life of 4.5 billion years.
